title: This Is Not Philosophy: The Article Economy and the Shape of the Field (EA-MMRS-TINP-01)
creator: Sharks, Lee
description: A census of twenty philosophy journals (ancient, continental, analytic) and two Persée series, coding each article's object and, from its abstract, what it does with that object, every code with a machine-checked verbatim span. In Ancient Philosophy 8 of 844 articles open the question of what the object is; since 2021, 4 of 283 Plato/Aristotle abstracts across the sister journals. The three fields are three placements of one unit, the article that places a position. In the Archiv für Geschichte der Philosophie of the 1890s one ancient title in five puts a work's standing in question; by the 1920s the question is gone from its pages; philology kept it longer and unevenly. A model asked for plausible abstracts reproduces each field's unit, raises its characteristic move, writes no claim about the text in sixty ancient abstracts, and deals one inventory of topics across mastheads. Disciplinarity is read as the stable form of the article economy; the editor's correspondence is read as the gate's specification of the unit. The texts are seated as EA-CORPORA-39 (#1771).
content_type: Journal article (Machine-Mediated Reception Studies); working notebook: census, reach study and model test
substrate: Human–machine collaborative. The study's question, predictions, title, subtitle, rulings and readings are Lee Sharks's, stated and dated in the text. The census, coding, measures, model-test analysis and drafting were done in session by TACHYON (Claude, Anthropic) under the author's direction; the reach codes were made by parallel Claude readers and the lead Claude instance, as §0.5b states, with agreement measured within that procedure only. The model test's abstracts were generated by ChatGPT, signed out, run by the author. Reviews by Gemini, DeepSeek and ChatGPT were checked point by point before any was applied. The Crimson Hexagonal Archive is credited as contributor: the measures read its seated texts (EA-CORPORA-39).
methodology: Crossref and Persée census of twenty-two series; object coding of titles by name lists; reach coding of every abstract on fixed codebooks (A–G), each code with a 6–30-word verbatim span machine-checked against the abstract, adjudicated in both directions; hand-ruled standing baselines from title-lexicon pulls; full-text measures of the seated Archiv, philology volumes and construction texts; coding of the Archiv articles' openings on the census codebook; stylometry on function words, a move lexicon and content vocabulary; a model test of 140 generated abstracts against the journals' own. All scripts and outputs are seated (EA-CORPORA-39/12) or attached (data/attachments/EA-MMRS-TINP-01/).
falsification_conditions: The study's figures are falsified if the census or codes do not rebuild from the seated scripts against Crossref and Persée; if a reach code's span is absent from its abstract; if the standing rulings are shown to misread their titles at a rate that changes the tables; if the full-text measures do not reproduce on the seated texts; or if repeated runs of the model test (each abstract generated separately, a second model, a perturbation prompt) return D at or above the field's rate. The reading of 2.3 and 5.6 fails if fields with a weaker credentialing economy show the same contraction of reach.

wiki_article: This Is Not Philosophy: The Article Economy and the Shape of the Field is a working notebook by Lee Sharks, deposited on 16 November 2026 as an article in Machine-Mediated Reception Studies and the second station of the archive's combined audit of the fields after Who Speaks for the Classics (#1770). It measures what the journals of philosophy publish. A census of twenty journals in Crossref, ancient (Ancient Philosophy, Phronesis, Apeiron, Elenchos, Rhizomata, the Archiv für Geschichte der Philosophie), continental and analytic, with two series harvested from Persée, codes each article's object and, from its abstract, what the article does with that object: re-read a passage, resolve an apparent inconsistency, reconstruct a doctrine, make a claim about the text itself, relate authors, carry the material past antiquity, or argue a position of its own. Each code carries a verbatim span from its abstract, checked by machine. In Ancient Philosophy, 8 of 844 articles open the question of what the object is; across the sister journals since 2021, 4 of 283 Plato and Aristotle abstracts do. The notebook reads the three fields as three placements of one unit, the article that places a position: the ancient field repairs a named object, the continental field pairs names, the analytic field takes a position in a debate, and the form of the abstract converges on the analytic. Its historical baseline is the Archiv für Geschichte der Philosophie of 1888–1924, where in the 1890s about one ancient title in five puts a work's authenticity, date or order in question and the pages carry the question at that rate until the First World War; by the 1920s it has left the journal's discussion of the ancients. The Revue philosophique de Louvain takes it up again as Jaeger's developmental question and lets it go after 1960; among the philology journals Philologus keeps it, while the Revue des Études Grecques and the Classical Quarterly let it go. A model test asks a language model for twenty plausible abstracts for each of seven journals; the generated abstracts reproduce each field's unit, raise its most characteristic move, contain no claim about the text in sixty ancient abstracts, and repeat one inventory of topics across the journals. The notebook argues that disciplinarity is the stable form of an article economy in which the journal certifies the person through a unit that cannot fail, and it reads the author's correspondence with the editor of Ancient Philosophy, in his official capacity, as the gate's own specification of that unit. It places itself in the archive's line on institutional model collapse (The Certified Center, The Wrong Unit) as the measurement those papers specified. The texts it reads are seated as EA-CORPORA-39 (#1771).
